analysis.one_liner: Strengthens civil rights and pollution-permit rules to protect communities of color from toxic pollution.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 105 Democratic cosponsors but died in six House committees without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let people sue when a federally funded program or practice has a discriminatory environmental effect on a community, require polluters seeking air and water permits to prove their discharge combined with existing pollution will not harm residents, and give federal agencies new duties to identify and fix disproportionate pollution burdens on communities of color, low-income communities, and Tribal and Indigenous communities. It would also fund parks, transit to trails, and grants for environmental justice work, and require ingredient labels on cosmetics and menstrual products. The bill never received a hearing or a vote in the 118th Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of communities that bear disproportionate pollution burdens — disproportionately communities of color, low-income communities, and Tribal and Indigenous communities — would gain new legal tools to challenge discriminatory effects, stricter permit standards that account for combined pollution exposure, park and recreation grants, safer-product labeling, and transition assistance for fossil-fuel-dependent workers.

how_it_helps.text: Expands Title VI of the Civil Rights Act so that federally funded programs and practices can be challenged for having a discriminatory effect based on race, color, or national origin, and gives aggrieved people the right to sue and recover attorney's fees and costs.

Requires air and water permits for major pollution sources to account for cumulative impacts — the combined pollution a community already experiences — and lets permitting authorities deny permits that cannot ensure a reasonable certainty of no harm, including from applicants with persistent violation histories.

Directs federal agencies to identify and address disproportionate health and environmental effects of their programs on communities of color, low-income communities, and Tribal and Indigenous communities, with public strategies, reporting, an EPA environmental justice ombuds, and a right to sue to enforce these duties.

Creates grant programs for parks and recreation in underserved urban areas, a transit-to-trails program, grants for environmental justice projects and tribal coastal zones, and research on safer alternatives to toxic chemicals in consumer, cleaning, toy, and baby products.

Requires ingredient labeling and warnings for certain products such as cosmetics and menstrual products, and directs agencies to strengthen environmental review for federal actions affecting environmental justice communities.

analysis.who_pays: Industrial facilities seeking air and water permits would face stricter cumulative-impact analyses, possible permit denials, and compliance plans; makers of cosmetics and menstrual products would bear labeling costs; and taxpayers would fund the new grant programs and advisory bodies. Fossil-fuel-dependent communities and workers would face economic pressure as the transition assistance is designed to offset.

drawbacks.text: Permitting authorities would have to deny or condition permits unless the applicant shows a reasonable certainty of no harm after cumulative-impact analysis, which could delay or block industrial projects and raise compliance costs for facilities, with possible effects on local jobs and prices.

Expanding disparate-impact liability under the Civil Rights Act with a private right of action would expose federally funded entities to new litigation, and the bill applies retroactively to pending actions on the date of enactment.

Grant programs for parks and transit-to-trails generally require recipients to provide matching funds equal to the grant, which can exclude the poorest communities unless the Secretary waives the requirement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades higher compliance costs and litigation risk for permitted industries and manufacturers against stronger legal protection and cleaner conditions for communities that today absorb disproportionate pollution, and the Communities affected would gain enforceable rights rather than only guidance. The main design questions are the breadth of the new permit-denial standard and the cost and delay it could impose on projects; the matching-fund requirements could limit access for the poorest communities.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to six House committees on the day it was introduced, then to several subcommittees, and no committee ever took it up, so it never reached the floor for a vote before the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Raúl Grijalva introduced the A. Donald McEachin Environmental Justice For All Act on March 22, 2023, with 34 original cosponsors including Ms. Lee of California, Ms. Tlaib, and Mr. Khanna.

It was referred to the Committees on Energy and Commerce, Natural Resources, Judiciary, Transportation and Infrastructure, Agriculture, and Education and the Workforce, and later to subcommittees including Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation, Highways and Transit, Water Resources and Environment, Environment Manufacturing and Critical Materials, and Forestry.
A total of 105 House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsor appears in the record.
The last recorded action was a subcommittee referral on April 25, 2023; no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote followed, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Facilities that would have faced stricter cumulative-impact permit reviews and possible permit denials, and federally funded entities that would have faced new disparate-impact suits, are better off because the bill never advanced. Residents of overburdened communities gained nothing from this outcome.

for.name: Raúl Grijalva
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited cosponsors.

against.name: House committee chairs (Energy and Commerce, Natural Resources, Judiciary, Transportation and Infrastructure, Agriculture, Education and the Workforce)
against.role: Committee chairs of the six committees of referral
against.what_they_did: None of the six committees took action on the bill after referral; no hearing or markup was ever held.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: House majority leadership in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor for a vote during the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 105 cosponsors were House Democrats, and no House Republican signed on; with Republicans holding the House majority and all committee chairs, the bill never advanced.

industries.industry: Permitted industrial polluters (power plants, factories, wastewater dischargers)
industries.note: The bill would require cumulative-impact analysis for air and water permits and let regulators deny permits that cannot ensure a reasonable certainty of no harm, directly limiting where and how heavily facilities may pollute in overburdened communities.

Stricter permitting and community impact review for federal actions affecting environmental justice communities would raise costs and risks for fossil fuel projects, while the bill funds economic transition assistance for fossil-fuel-dependent communities and workers.

industries.industry: Cosmetics and personal care product makers
industries.note: The bill requires ingredient listing and warnings for cosmetics and menstrual products and funds research into safer alternatives, imposing labeling and reformulation costs.

industries.industry: Environmental justice, Tribal, and community organizations
industries.note: The bill channels new grants, advisory seats, technical assistance, and a right of action to organizations working in overburdened communities.

industries.industry: State and local park and transit agencies
industries.note: New grant programs for urban parks, transit-to-trails routes, and recreation in underserved communities would flow to state, local, and Tribal entities.
